To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant Salmonella in raw, chilled chicken in retail outlets was high, but the level of multiple resistance was relatively low, that imported chicken breast fillet was less resistant than locally produced chicken, and that there was no significant difference between the resistance profiles of imported chicken breast and human fecal isolations.

the antimicrobial resistance patterns of Salmonella isolates obtained from retail chickens and human clinical specimens in the UK were more similar to each other than to those of imported chicken portions.
Salmonella from raw chicken, imported chicken, and human fecal specimens are resistant to multiple antibiotics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevalence and patterns of antimicrobial resistance in salmonellas in raw retail chicken, chicken breast fillets from Brazil and Thailand, and human clinical isolates.
the antimicrobial susceptibility of Salmonella in retail chickens, chicken breast portions imported from Thailand and Brazil, and human clinical isolates.
the prevalence of antibiotic resistant salmonellas isolated from retail raw chickens, imported chicken breast fillettes and human clinical samples.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a low level of multiple antibiotic resistance in salmonellas in raw chicken meat in this country and that the imported salmonellas are less resistant than those from locally reared chickens.

there is no significant difference in resistance patterns between human clinical isolates and those of raw retail chickens, but that imported chicken portions show a lower level of resistance to sulfonamide and streptomycin.

resistance in imported salmonella isolates is not significantly different from that of local isolates, but that the overall level of antimicrobial resistance in imported chicken portions was lower than that in nonimported chicken.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the resistance of salmonellas in raw chicken is a problem that is not confined to imported chicken.
the resistance of Salmonella isolates in imported chicken portions from Brazil and Thailand is generally less than in locally produced chicken and in human clinical isolates.

resistance to sulfonamides, streptomycin, tetracycline, and ampicillin was the most prevalent in salmonellas from raw retail chickens, but that the majority of imported chicken breast portions were resistant to only one antibiotic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of antibiotics in food animals is contributing to resistance in salmonellas, and this is reflected in the prevalence of resistance in human salmonella isolates.
the resistance of salmonellas in imported chicken is not necessarily greater than that in locally produced chicken.

imported chicken is a much lower risk than local chicken in terms of antimicrobial resistance, although it should be borne in mind that the local chickens were raw retail products, whereas the imported chicken was mainly frozen portions.
